title: Association Rules
summary: Count what occurs together. Follow the denominators, prune the search, and judge what a rule can really tell you.
intro: Four baskets. Two denominators. A whole way to discover what goes together. Work through your Week 03 lecture, seminar, textbook, and Python practical with drawings you can change.
prerequisite: Fractions, percentages, and reading a small table. Python is optional until section 20.
next: Which patterns survive a threshold, and which deserve a decision?

stages.title: A basket becomes a row
stages.question: What exactly are we counting?
stages.answerHtml: A transaction is one observed basket. An item is a product, and an itemset is a group of products. We ask how many baskets contain every item in the group. Each basket counts once, regardless of how many units of a product it contains.
stages.receiptHtml:
The recurring lecture dataset

TID (transaction ID)Items in the basket
100Apple, Coke, DVD
200Bread, Coke, Egg
300Apple, Bread, Coke, Egg
400Bread, Egg

A = Apple, B = Bread, C = Coke, D = DVD, E = Egg. These short labels identify the products in the drawings.

A Boolean row records presence: 1 = present, 0 = absent. TID identifies the row and is never a product.

Source basis: Lecture p.11; seminar slide 11. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Select basket 400. Predict what changes if you add Coke, then tick Coke. Follow that same change through the next sections. Reset restores the four source baskets.
stages.whyHtml:
The notebook uses A = Apple, B = Bread, C = Coke, D = DVD, E = Egg when a drawing needs short labels. A 3-itemset contains three distinct items.

Define the transaction unit before mining. A receipt, a customer across a month, and a single product record answer different questions. Repeated appearances of the same item in a basket do not increase its Boolean support.

The practical uses MP3 in place of the lecture’s DVD. The pattern of presence is the same in the four displayed source rows, but the names identify different products.
stages.check: If a basket has three apples, does it count three times toward Apple support?
stages.solution: No. For Boolean association mining it is one basket containing Apple, so it contributes one count.
stages.referent: Four outlined baskets contain product chips; the selected basket becomes a Boolean presence row.
stages.action: Select a basket and change its item checkboxes
stages.nextReason: Now use these same baskets to ask a question with two sides.

stages.title: A rule has two sides
stages.question: What does Apple → Coke actually claim?
stages.answerHtml: Apple → Coke reads: among baskets containing Apple, how often does Coke also appear? Apple is the antecedent X, and Coke is the consequent Y. The two sides must be nonempty and share no items. The joint count counts baskets containing every item from both sides.
stages.receiptHtml:
Read the arrow as a conditional question

X = {Apple}
Y = {Coke}
X ∪ Y = {Apple, Coke}

Both Apple baskets, 100 and 300, also contain Coke. The arrow gives a direction for counting. It does not establish what happened first.

Source basis: Lecture pp.13–14. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Switch from Apple → Coke to Bread + Coke → Egg. Identify the baskets that qualify for the left side before inspecting their Egg marks.
stages.whyHtml:
A transaction satisfies X only when it contains every item in X. Bread + Coke means an AND condition, not an either/or condition.

The notation X ∪ Y combines the item names into one set. Its support counts baskets that contain all those names. In probability language, this is the intersection of the events “contains X” and “contains Y”.

Association rules describe co-occurrence. A rule by itself establishes neither a causal effect nor statistical dependence. Lift later compares the co-occurrence with an independence baseline.
stages.check: Can Apple + Coke → Coke be a valid association rule here?
stages.solution: No. Coke appears on both sides. The antecedent and consequent must be disjoint, otherwise the right side is partly guaranteed by the left.
stages.referent: Aligned TID rows show antecedent membership, consequent membership and their joint matches.
stages.action: Choose a rule and inspect the qualifying rows
stages.nextReason: The rule names the two sides. Next choose which baskets belong in its denominator.

stages.title: Support counts everybody
stages.question: Which denominator belongs to support?
stages.answerHtml: Support is the fraction of all transactions that contain the itemset. A rule’s support uses the combined set X ∪ Y: the union of the item names from both sides. Its denominator is the entire dataset, including baskets containing neither side.
stages.receiptHtml:
All four baskets are in the denominator

count({Apple, Coke}) = 2
support(Apple → Coke) = 2/4 = 50%

Baskets 100 and 300 are the two joint matches. Baskets 200 and 400 still belong to the denominator, even though they do not contain Apple.

Source basis: Lecture pp.13–17; recurring four-basket example. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Choose Bread → Egg. Count the green baskets before reading the fraction. Compare its support with Apple → Coke.
stages.whyHtml:
Support count is an absolute number of transactions. Relative support divides that count by N, the total number of transactions. A minimum count of 2 is 50% in four baskets but 2% in one hundred baskets.

The combined itemset is unordered. Apple → Coke and Coke → Apple have the same support because they count the same co-occurrences.

Adding baskets that contain neither item leaves the numerator unchanged and enlarges the denominator. Section 15 makes this visible.

A separate six-person lecture exampleJoint count / all people
Banana → Chicken1 / 6 = 16.7%
Coffee → Milk3 / 6 = 50%

These extra examples use a different six-person dataset. Their denominator is six, not the four baskets in the live lab.
stages.check: Is 2/2 the support of Apple → Coke in the source dataset?
stages.solution: No. 2/2 restricts the denominator to Apple baskets, which asks a different question. Support includes all four baskets, so it is 2/4. The next section explains that smaller denominator.
stages.referent: Four transaction slots retain the full denominator; the matching slots and support fraction reconcile.
stages.action: Change the rule and count its joint matches
stages.nextReason: The joint count stays two. Next restrict the denominator to Apple baskets.

stages.title: Confidence zooms into X
stages.question: Why does confidence change the denominator?
stages.answerHtml: Confidence restricts attention to baskets containing X. It measures the fraction of those baskets that also contain Y. First choose the group on the left of the arrow, then count successes inside it.
stages.receiptHtml:
A smaller group, the same joint count

confidence(Apple → Coke)
= count({Apple, Coke}) / count({Apple})
= 2/2 = 100%

All four baskets supplied the support denominator. Now keep only baskets 100 and 300, the two Apple baskets. Both also contain Coke.

Source basis: Lecture pp.15–17. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Choose Bread → Coke. Three baskets contain Bread. Which one fails the consequent? Watch it remain in the confidence denominator.
stages.whyHtml:
In probability notation confidence is P(Y | X). The vertical bar means “given X”. It is an empirical conditional proportion in these observed transactions, not a guarantee for the next customer.

When no basket contains X, the denominator is zero and confidence is undefined. The notebook displays “Undefined” if an edit creates that case.

High confidence can arise simply because Y is common. We need the baseline support of Y before judging how surprising the rule is.

In the separate six-person lecture example, three of the four Coffee buyers also buy Milk: confidence is 3/4 = 75%. The joint count is still three, while support uses all six people: 3/6 = 50%.
stages.check: If three baskets contain X and two contain both X and Y, what is confidence?
stages.solution: 2/3, or about 66.7%. A basket with X but without Y remains in the denominator and counts as a failure.
stages.referent: The conditioning cohort contains only X baskets; green successes supply the numerator and bar length.
stages.action: Change X and locate its success and failure baskets
stages.nextReason: The left side chose the denominator. Next reverse the arrow and choose a different group.

stages.title: Reversing the arrow
stages.question: What stays the same when we reverse a rule?
stages.answerHtml: Reversing the arrow keeps the joint count and support unchanged. Confidence usually changes because we divide by a different group: Apple baskets in one direction and Coke baskets in the other.
stages.receiptHtml:
Two directions, one pair

RuleSupportConfidence
Apple → Coke2/4 = 50%2/2 = 100%
Coke → Apple2/4 = 50%2/3 = 66.7%

The same two baskets are successful in both directions. They fill all 2 Apple places, but only 2 of the 3 Coke places.

Source basis: Lecture dataset; seminar review slides 53–54. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Compare the two equal-sized basket slots in each row. Predict what changes when you switch Apple → Coke to Coke → Apple. The successful basket IDs stay the same; only the qualifying group changes.
stages.whyHtml:
For disjoint X and Y, support(X → Y) = support(Y → X). Confidence(X → Y) uses count(X), while confidence(Y → X) uses count(Y).

A rule’s direction expresses the question the analyst asks. It does not encode the order of purchase. Sequential pattern mining introduces order as a separate concept.

The GPU seminar example is another useful contrast: CPU → GPU has 20% confidence, while GPU → CPU has 80%, using the same 1,200 joint purchases.
stages.check: If confidence in both directions is equal and the joint count is positive, what follows?
stages.solution: The antecedent and consequent counts are equal. With the same positive numerator, equal fractions require equal denominators.
stages.referent: Two different conditioning cohorts display the same joint basket IDs but different denominators.
stages.action: Choose the forward and reverse rules
stages.nextReason: A high confidence may simply reflect a common product. Next compare it with the overall baseline.

stages.title: Lift checks the baseline
stages.question: Can high confidence still hide a weaker association?
stages.answerHtml: Confidence describes the X group. We now compare it with how common Y is overall: the baseline is support(Y). Lift = confidence / baseline. Below 1 means Y is less common in the X group; above 1 means it is more common. At 1, the two groups have the same Y rate.
stages.receiptHtml:
Basketball and cereal: the source counterexample

N = 5,000; Basketball = 3,000
Cereal = 3,750; Both = 2,000
confidence = 2,000/3,000 = 66.7%
baseline = 3,750/5,000 = 75%
lift = (2/3)/(3/4) = 8/9 ≈ 0.89

With independent occurrence we would expect 3,000 × 3,750 / 5,000 = 2,250 joint records. We observe only 2,000.

Source basis: Lecture p.49; seminar slides 51–52. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Keep the group sizes fixed and move the joint count to 2,250. Predict the lift before reading it. Then choose the CPU or burger example to check another source calculation.
stages.whyHtml:
Lift is symmetric when both itemsets have positive support: lift(X → Y) = support(X ∪ Y) / [support(X) × support(Y)]. For Apple and Coke, this is (2/4) / [(2/4) × (3/4)] = 4/3 ≈ 1.33 in either direction.

Lift above 1 indicates positive dependence relative to the marginal frequencies. Lift below 1 indicates negative dependence. Exactly 1 corresponds to empirical independence for these two binary events when both margins are positive.

A value near 1 in a finite sample is not proof of independence in a population. Lift also does not estimate the effect of a promotion or a recommendation.

The permitted joint count is bounded: max(0, count(X) + count(Y) − N) ≤ count(X ∪ Y) ≤ min(count(X), count(Y)). The slider respects those bounds.

The practical’s Burger → Ketchup example gives 5% rule support, 33.3% confidence, and lift 3.33. Ketchup’s 10% support is the consequent baseline, not the rule support.
stages.check: The cereal confidence is 66.7%. Is that above its 75% baseline?
stages.solution: No. Lift is about 0.89. Cereal occurs less often among basketball players than it does overall. The arrow does not imply basketball causes that difference.
stages.referent: Two percentage bars compare conditional occurrence and baseline; observed and expected joint counts reconcile.
stages.action: Move co-occurrence while retaining the source margins
stages.nextReason: Lift describes the baseline comparison. Next decide which support and confidence levels a rule must pass.

stages.title: A strong rule meets two cutoffs
stages.question: How do minimum support and confidence work together?
stages.answerHtml: An itemset is frequent when it passes minimum support. A strong rule passes both minimum support and minimum confidence. First find frequent itemsets, then filter the rules made from them. Equality at a cutoff counts as passing.
stages.receiptHtml:
Source defaults: support ≥ 50%, confidence ≥ 90%

Candidate ruleSupportConfidencePasses both?
Apple → Coke50%100%Yes
Coke → Apple50%66.7%No
Bread → Egg75%100%Yes

The lecture dataset produces 9 frequent itemsets and 5 strong rules at these cutoffs.

Source basis: Lecture pp.26–28. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Predict which red points turn green when you lower minimum confidence to 65%. Then raise minimum support to 75%: watch the same rule positions remain on the map while the lower-support ones fail. Check the table of rules that pass both.
stages.whyHtml:
The five source rules at 50% support and 90% confidence are Apple → Coke, Bread → Egg, Egg → Bread, Bread + Coke → Egg, and Coke + Egg → Bread.

A higher support cutoff never adds a new frequent itemset on fixed data. A lower confidence cutoff can add rules once their itemsets already pass support.

“Strong” is a threshold definition. It says nothing by itself about usefulness, novelty, causal effect, or statistical significance. Low support can expose rare patterns but usually increases candidate and output volume.

The map includes rules from every combination seen in at least one current basket, so a rejected point stays visible. A numeral groups rules with identical support and confidence. The table names the rules that pass both cutoffs.
stages.check: A rule has 49% support and 100% confidence. Does it pass a 50% support threshold?
stages.solution: No. Both conditions must pass. Perfect confidence cannot compensate for insufficient support.
stages.referent: A support/confidence map retains every positive observed rule when cutoffs change; grouped numerals show coincident rules.
stages.action: Move both threshold lines and inspect the surviving rules
stages.nextReason: To find qualifying rules, first find frequent itemsets. The next property lets us avoid impossible branches.

stages.title: Apriori prunes supersets
stages.question: Why can an infrequent subset stop a whole branch?
stages.answerHtml: Bread + Coke is a subset of Bread + Coke + Egg; the triple is a superset because it adds Egg. Adding requirements can only keep or reduce the matching baskets. Every basket containing the triple also contains the pair, so the triple’s support count cannot be larger.
stages.receiptHtml:
The downward closure property

count({Bread, Coke, Egg}) = 2
count({Bread, Coke}) = 2
count({Bread}) = 3

DVD appears once. At a minimum count of 2, every itemset containing DVD must fail. We can discard those branches before counting them.

Source basis: Lecture pp.21–24; textbook §6.2.1. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Inspect Bread + Coke + Egg, then Apple + Bread + Coke. Compare each pair subset with the complete set. Find a failing subset that rules out the triple.
stages.whyHtml:
The Apriori property says every nonempty subset of a frequent itemset is frequent at the same threshold. Its useful contrapositive says an infrequent itemset has no frequent superset.

The converse fails: frequent singletons do not ensure a frequent pair, and frequent pairs do not ensure a frequent triple. Different subsets can occur in different baskets.

Confidence lacks this general support property. A confidence threshold cannot be substituted for minimum support in arbitrary candidate pruning.
stages.check: If Apple and Bread are frequent separately, must Apple + Bread be frequent?
stages.solution: No. In the four source baskets both singletons pass count 2, but their pair appears only in basket 300 and fails.
stages.referent: Aligned basket slots make subset inclusion and the non-increasing match count visible.
stages.action: Choose an itemset and compare it with its immediate subsets
stages.nextReason: Turn that counting property into Apriori’s join, prune and count procedure.

stages.title: Apriori joins, prunes, counts
stages.question: How does the algorithm build longer patterns?
stages.answerHtml: Apriori works one itemset length at a time. Cₖ means candidates of length k. Lₖ means candidates that passed support. Join the previous frequent sets, reject missing-subset candidates, then scan the baskets to count survivors.
stages.receiptHtml:
The lecture’s four-basket trace, count ≥ 2

LevelFrequent sets (support count)
L₁A:2, B:3, C:3, E:3
L₂AC:2, BC:2, BE:3, CE:2
L₃BCE:2
L₄Empty, so stop
Join BC + BE → BCE
Check BC, BE, CE in L₂
Count matching baskets 200 and 300 → 2
2 meets the cutoff → keep BCE in L₃

A = Apple, B = Bread, C = Coke, D = DVD, E = Egg. Candidate counts include AB:1 and AE:1, which fail the scan.

Source basis: Lecture pp.23–28; textbook §§6.2.1–6.2.3. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Start at level 3: BC and BE join to form BCE, and CE must also pass the subset check. Step back to level 2 and inspect AB, which fails after counting. To see pruning before counting, lower support to 25%, return to level 3, and inspect ADE: DE is missing from the frequent pairs.
stages.whyHtml:
Sort item names consistently. Two frequent (k − 1)-sets can join when their first k − 2 items match. The joined set must have k distinct items. Check every immediate (k − 1)-subset against Lₖ₋₁ before scanning.

The supplied lecture’s A,C,D / B,C,E example is the same pattern of item presence as our named baskets, with D corresponding to DVD.

Apriori can require many database scans and create many candidates. Hash buckets can rule out low-count groups, transaction reduction skips rows that cannot hold longer frequent sets, partitioning collects local candidates then verifies them globally, and sampling trades completeness for speed unless followed by suitable verification. Dynamic counting introduces candidates within a scan.

With the default 50% support, BCE is the only triple generated by the ordered join. Apple triples are already blocked by missing frequent pairs. At 25% support, AD and AE can join into ADE, but DE has count zero: the subset check prunes ADE without scanning it.
stages.check: All immediate subsets passed. Can we output the candidate as frequent without counting it?
stages.solution: No. Passing the subset test only makes it a viable candidate. Its own count still has to meet minimum support.
stages.referent: Parent chips join into a candidate; all immediate subsets are checked; qualifying baskets are counted only if pruning permits.
stages.action: Advance the candidate length and move minimum support
stages.nextReason: The frequent itemsets are ready. Next divide each one into possible rule sides.

stages.title: An itemset becomes several rules
stages.question: Why does BCE produce six possible rules?
stages.answerHtml: Apriori has found itemsets; now we turn a chosen itemset into rules. Choose a nonempty part as the antecedent X and put the remaining items in consequent Y. For k items there are 2ᵏ − 2 splits: two choices per item, excluding an empty side. Support stays fixed; confidence denominators can differ.
stages.receiptHtml:
Split {Bread, Coke, Egg}, whose count is 2

RuleConfidencePasses 90%?
Bread → Coke + Egg2/3 = 66.7%No
Coke → Bread + Egg2/3 = 66.7%No
Egg → Bread + Coke2/3 = 66.7%No
Bread + Coke → Egg2/2 = 100%Yes
Bread + Egg → Coke2/3 = 66.7%No
Coke + Egg → Bread2/2 = 100%Yes

Source basis: Lecture p.28; textbook §6.2.2. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Move the split slider and watch the same item chips move between X and Y. For BCE, predict each denominator from the basket IDs, then lower confidence to 65%. Try a five-item set to see 30 possible splits; some have no qualifying antecedent baskets.
stages.whyHtml:
The empty antecedent and empty consequent account for the two excluded subsets in 2ᵏ − 2. A consequent can contain multiple items, which must all be present.

The itemset must pass support before any of its rules can be strong. This scene shows possible splits even when a live edit or threshold makes the chosen itemset infrequent, and marks them as failing support.

Rule generation is a separate step from frequent-itemset mining. Apriori and FP-growth can feed the same rule-generation routine when their itemsets and counts agree.
stages.check: For Bread + Egg → Coke, should the denominator be the count of Bread alone?
stages.solution: No. Count baskets containing both Bread and Egg. In the source dataset that is 3, so confidence is 2/3.
stages.referent: The combined item chips partition into X and Y; qualifying antecedent basket IDs reveal each split’s confidence denominator.
stages.action: Walk through all disjoint splits of the chosen itemset
stages.nextReason: Apriori found the patterns by scanning candidates. Next see a different way to store the baskets.

stages.title: FP-trees share prefixes
stages.question: How can five baskets fit into a compact tree?
stages.answerHtml: Apriori repeatedly builds candidates. An FP-tree instead compresses baskets into shared ordered paths. First remove infrequent items and choose one global frequency order. A prefix is the shared starting part of a path. Insert each filtered basket; reuse its existing prefix and increase those node counts.
stages.receiptHtml:
A separate FP-tree example from the lecture

TIDFrequent items in global order
100f, c, a, m, p
200f, c, a, b, m
300f, b
400c, b, p
500f, c, a, m, p
Minimum support count = 3
Header: f:4, c:4, a:3, b:3, m:3, p:3

Here f, c, a, b, m and p are abstract item labels in a separate five-basket dataset, not the Apple–Egg abbreviations.

The header lists each item’s count across all five baskets. In the tree, ∅ is the empty root where paths start, not an item. Each node label is item:prefix count. The f → c node’s c:3 counts three baskets with that prefix; c:1 on another branch accounts for c’s fourth occurrence.

Both f and c occur four times. The lecture chooses f before c to break that tie. Keep the same order in every basket.

Source basis: Lecture pp.33–35; seminar slides 35–37. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Set inserted baskets to 0, then step through 1 to 5. Follow each raw basket through filtering and ordering into its gold tree path. On the last step, compare c:3 + c:1 in the tree with global c:4 in the header.
stages.whyHtml:
A node count is the number of inserted transactions that share the complete path from the root to that node. It is not necessarily the item’s global support count. The two c nodes carry counts 3 and 1, which add to header c:4.

The first original-data scan obtains support and order. The second constructs the tree. Item header links connect nodes for the same item across branches. The gold inspection highlights the latest inserted path.

Compression depends on common prefixes. FP-growth avoids explicit candidate generation and is often efficient on large data, but branching and conditional trees can still demand substantial memory. “Faster” is not a universal runtime guarantee.
stages.check: Does the f → c node’s c:3 mean c appears only three times in all five baskets?
stages.solution: No. It counts the f,c prefix. Another c:1 starts at the root, so c’s global count is 4.
stages.referent: Raw item chips are filtered and globally ordered, then the latest inserted path is traced through counted tree nodes.
stages.action: Insert source transactions one at a time
stages.nextReason: The tree has stored the baskets. Next trace prefixes to extract patterns ending in one chosen item.

stages.title: FP-growth follows a suffix
stages.question: Where does a conditional pattern base come from?
stages.answerHtml: The tree is built; now we extract patterns from it. Pick a suffix, the last item of a pattern in the chosen global order. Follow each matching tree node toward the root. Remove the suffix and keep each prefix with that suffix node’s count as its weight: this is the conditional pattern base.
stages.receiptHtml:
Mine the lecture’s m suffix, count ≥ 3

Conditional base for m:
f, c, a : weight 2
f, c, a, b : weight 1

Conditional counts: f:3, c:3, a:3, b:1
Remove b; conditional path is f:3 → c:3 → a:3

The projection uses only items earlier than m in the global order. Append m to each nonempty combination of f, c, a. Together with m itself, this gives 8 patterns generated in the m projection.

Source basis: Lecture pp.34–35; textbook §6.2.4. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: For m, trace the two gold suffix nodes back to the root. Predict the two prefix weights before reading their receipts. Change m to p, and follow the weighted counts into the conditional tree. Notice why a globally frequent item can fail inside this projection.
stages.whyHtml:
The prefix f,c,a occurs on a node path whose m count is 2, so it contributes weight 2. Using the ancestor f count of 4 would overcount transactions that never reached that m.

Construct a conditional FP-tree from the weighted base, remove infrequent items using the same absolute support threshold, and recurse. A single path permits direct combination enumeration. A branching tree needs further conditional mining.

The drawing shows the complete five-transaction source tree’s conditional base, regardless of the insertion position chosen in the previous section. It labels that scope explicitly.

Here a suffix is the last item of a pattern in the global order. Its conditional base contains earlier items only. Patterns involving a later item are generated in that later item’s projection, so changing the suffix does not list every pattern containing the chosen item.
stages.check: In the m base, b appears with weight 1. Does b’s global support of 3 let it survive?
stages.solution: No. Conditional support must also reach 3. Only one transaction in the m projection includes b.
stages.referent: Gold source-tree paths expose suffix counts; the exact weights form a conditional base, weighted totals and conditional tree.
stages.action: Choose a suffix and inspect its weighted prefix counts
stages.nextReason: FP-growth reused tree paths. Next reuse transaction-ID lists instead.

stages.title: Eclat intersects transaction IDs
stages.question: Can we count a pair without scanning every basket again?
stages.answerHtml: We can also reuse counts without a prefix tree. In a vertical format, each itemset stores the IDs of baskets containing it. Intersect two ID lists: keep only IDs in both. Their number is the combined itemset’s support count. Eclat grows patterns using these intersections.
stages.receiptHtml:
Keep only the IDs common to both lists

Apple: {100, 300}
Coke: {100, 200, 300}
Intersection: {100, 300}
count({Apple, Coke}) = 2

Source basis: Textbook §6.2.5, adapted to the recurring lecture data. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Switch to Bread → Coke. Read the two ID lanes and predict their intersection. Compare the result with the pair’s support count in Apriori.
stages.whyHtml:
The first transformation scans the baskets to build the ID sets. Later support calculations can reuse intersections instead of scanning the original rows repeatedly.

For multiple items, intersect all their ID sets. Within an antecedent such as Bread + Coke, its own ID set is already an intersection.

Long ID lists can consume memory and intersection time. Diffsets can store the IDs lost when extending a parent pattern. In the Apple/Coke example no Apple ID is lost, so the diffset relative to Apple is empty.
stages.check: Apple appears in two IDs, and Coke in three. Should their pair count be 2 + 3?
stages.solution: No. Only shared IDs qualify. Here the intersection has two IDs. Adding counts would count baskets that contain just one side and duplicate shared baskets.
stages.referent: Aligned transaction IDs show each side and their intersection; shared IDs supply the combined support count.
stages.action: Choose a rule and intersect the two sides’ ID sets
stages.nextReason: We can mine many patterns. Next see which ones preserve information without keeping every subset.

stages.title: Frequent, closed, maximal
stages.question: Which patterns can we keep without losing support information?
stages.answerHtml: Many frequent patterns repeat the same information. A closed frequent itemset has no larger itemset with the same count. A maximal frequent itemset has no frequent larger itemset at all. Keep closed patterns with their counts to recover exact supports of all frequent subsets; maximal patterns generally preserve only which subsets are frequent.
stages.receiptHtml:
The seminar’s three-transaction exercise, count ≥ 2

TIDItems
10A, B, C
20B, C, D
30A, C
FamilyPatterns and counts
FrequentA:2, B:2, C:3, AC:2, BC:2
ClosedC:3, AC:2, BC:2
MaximalAC:2, BC:2

A and AC both occur in baskets 10 and 30. Adding C loses no baskets, so we can keep AC:2 and recover A’s count of 2. C:3 needs its own record because its frequent extensions have count 2. Keeping only maximal AC:2 and BC:2 would lose the information that C occurs three times.

Source basis: Seminar slides 57–61; lecture pp.37–41. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Inspect A in the inclusion diagram: AC has the same count, so A is not closed. Inspect C: both frequent extensions have smaller counts. Try the family filter and change minimum count.
stages.whyHtml:
A larger itemset that contains X is a proper superset of X. Every maximal frequent itemset is closed, but a closed itemset may still have a frequent extension.

The little letters A–D belong to the seminar’s separate abstract dataset. They are not product abbreviations in this scene. Lines connect immediate set extensions that are present in the data.

Closed frequent sets and their counts retain the supports of all frequent subsets: the support of X is the maximum count of a closed frequent superset containing X. Maximal sets tell us which subsets are frequent but generally do not preserve their exact counts.

A frequent set of 100 items has 2¹⁰⁰ − 1 nonempty subsets. Direct closed-pattern miners can merge items always appearing together, prune sub-itemsets with matching support, skip redundant projections, and check closure, rather than enumerate everything and filter afterward.

At confidence 90%, the seminar’s final strong rules are A → C and B → C. The displayed reverse candidates C → A and C → B have 2/3 confidence and fail the stated cutoff.
stages.check: Is C closed and maximal in the seminar exercise?
stages.solution: C is closed because no proper superset has its count of 3. It is not maximal because AC and BC are frequent with count 2.
stages.referent: An inclusion diagram classifies patterns; selected and extension basket IDs explain same-count closure and support reconstruction.
stages.action: Inspect a pattern, filter the family, and change minimum count
stages.nextReason: We have summarized patterns and counts. Next see how changing the background affects their scores.

stages.title: Null transactions change some scores
stages.question: What happens if many baskets contain neither item?
stages.answerHtml: We have counted and summarized patterns. Now check what happens when the background changes. A null transaction contains neither X nor Y. Adding such rows increases the all-basket denominator N, changing support and lift. The X and Y groups stay the same, so both directional confidences stay fixed.
stages.receiptHtml:
A small teaching example inspired by Chapter 6

Both = 10, X only = 10, Y only = 10
With 0 null rows: N=30, lift=0.75
With 10 null rows: N=40, lift=1.00
With 100 null rows: N=130, lift=3.25
In all three: conf(X→Y)=conf(Y→X)=0.50

These are constructed counts, not measured customers. The point is to hold the co-occurrence evidence fixed while changing the background.

Source basis: Textbook §6.3.3, null-invariance discussion. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Predict what 100 extra neither rows will do, then add them. Watch blank circles enter the population and support shrink while the X-conditioned confidence stays at 50%. Increase Y-only rows next and compare the two confidence denominators. Open the optional score table for other overlap measures.
stages.whyHtml:
A measure is null-invariant if extra neither rows leave it unchanged while all other counts stay fixed. Confidence, all-confidence, max-confidence, Kulczynski, cosine and the imbalance ratio have this property.

Let c₁ = P(Y|X), c₂ = P(X|Y). All-confidence is min(c₁,c₂), max-confidence is max(c₁,c₂), Kulczynski (Kulc) is (c₁+c₂)/2, and cosine is √(c₁c₂). Each lies between 0 and 1 when defined.

IR = |count(X) − count(Y)|
/ [count(X)+count(Y)−count(X∪Y)]

The IR denominator counts rows containing at least one of X or Y. IR = 0 means balanced marginal counts. A large IR warns that the two directions can be very different. Kulc and IR together describe overlap and imbalance.

Null-invariant does not mean every change to the population should be ignored. Lift answers a baseline-relative question; the other scores answer different questions. Kulc = 0.5 is not a general proof of statistical independence.
stages.check: Does adding a null transaction count as a failure among X baskets?
stages.solution: No. It contains no X and never enters the X-conditioned denominator. It does enter the full N denominator for support and baseline frequency.
stages.referent: One circle per constructed transaction shows both, each single side and added blank neither rows; three percentage bars show changing and fixed denominators.
stages.action: Add null rows and separately change the imbalance
stages.nextReason: Confidence stayed fixed while the baseline moved. Next compare observed and expected counts in all four cells.

stages.title: Observed versus expected
stages.question: What does the χ² calculation add?
stages.answerHtml: Lift compared observed and expected joint occurrence. Pearson’s chi-square (χ²) statistic compares all four cells: both, X only, Y only and neither. Each contributes (observed − expected)² / expected. Add the four nonnegative contributions to obtain χ².
stages.receiptHtml:
The textbook’s games/videos table

CellObservedExpected
Games + videos4,0004,500
Games only2,0001,500
Videos only3,5003,000
Neither5001,000
Expected joint = 6,000×7,500/10,000 = 4,500
First contribution = (4,000−4,500)²/4,500
≈ 55.56
χ² = 55.56 + 166.67 + 83.33 + 250
≈ 555.56

Source basis: Textbook Examples 6.8–6.9, pp.266–267. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: The lab starts with Games / videos, matching this table. Move the joint count from 4,000 to 4,500. Keep both group totals fixed and predict what happens to all four signed differences and squared contributions. Restore 4,000 afterward.
stages.whyHtml:
Each expected cell is its row total times its column total divided by N. The figure shows observed and expected counts on one shared count scale. The table shows the four separate contributions.

χ² alone has no positive or negative direction. Compare observed joint count with expected joint count to describe the direction. A large statistic is also sensitive to sample size. Like lift, χ² can change when extra neither rows are added.

A significance claim needs a test setup, degrees of freedom, assumptions, a chosen error rate, and, where relevant, corrections for many mined hypotheses. For a nondegenerate 2×2 table the usual degrees of freedom is 1. χ² > 1 is not a general significance rule. This notebook reports the uncorrected Pearson statistic and no p-value.
stages.check: Can a squared χ² contribution be negative when observed is below expected?
stages.solution: No. The signed discrepancy is negative, but its square is nonnegative. The direction of association must be read from observed versus expected joint counts.
stages.referent: Four observed/expected bar pairs share a count scale; signed differences become nonnegative squared contributions and a sum.
stages.action: Compare source cohorts and move their joint counts
stages.nextReason: Scores help judge a rule. Next constrain the search to itemsets that answer an allowed question.

stages.title: Constraints direct the search
stages.question: When can a budget rule prune longer itemsets?
stages.answerHtml: Scores judge discovered rules. Constraints tell the search which itemsets are allowed. An anti-monotone constraint lets us stop after a failure: every larger set fails too. A monotone constraint preserves success as we add items. For sum constraints, the item values matter.
stages.receiptHtml:
The lecture’s nonnegative item values

Itemabcdefgh
Value400201030302010
Upper budget: sum(S) ≤ 35
{a,d} costs 50, so it fails.
Every extension still costs at least 50.

Lower target: sum(S) ≥ 35
{a,d} passes. Every extension still passes.
Range = largest value − smallest value
For {a,d}: 40−10 = 30
Adding b:0 widens the range to 40−0 = 40

Source basis: Lecture pp.52–56,61; seminar slides 64–73. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Inspect {a,d} and its extensions. For sum constraints, the gold segment is the added item’s value. Switch to upper range: the bracket spans the smallest to largest value. Predict which passing or failing outcomes must persist before changing the bound.
stages.whyHtml:
Nonnegative values make sum(S) ≤ v anti-monotone and sum(S) ≥ v monotone. A negative item could repair an upper-budget failure, so the pruning would become invalid.

range(S) = max(S) − min(S) cannot shrink as a nonempty set grows. An upper range bound is anti-monotone. A lower range bound is monotone.

A succinct constraint can be enforced by generating only allowed items or itemsets before support counting. For example, max(price) ≤ 120 lets us exclude individually expensive items first.

Convertible constraints can gain a useful pruning property along a chosen item order. Average-value constraints are a key example, but the exact order and direction must be justified. Inconvertible constraints lack such a usable conversion in the specified domain. Sums with unrestricted negative and positive values can lose both simple monotonicity properties.

Apply a valid constraint early when it saves work. Filtering completed output alone produces fewer displayed patterns but does not undo the mining cost.
stages.check: Could adding an item with value −30 repair a set that costs 50 under an upper budget of 35?
stages.solution: Yes. The new sum is 20. That is why nonnegative item values are an explicit assumption for upper-sum anti-monotone pruning.
stages.referent: Sum bars expose parent and added values; range dots and a min–max bracket are separated from the zero-based range-length comparison with the bound.
stages.action: Change the constraint, bound, and parent set
stages.nextReason: A budget is one kind of condition. Next consider items that belong to broader and narrower categories.

stages.title: Categories have different levels
stages.question: Why can one support threshold hide a whole subtype?
stages.answerHtml: A broad category occurs at least as often as any of its subtypes. A uniform support cutoff can keep Milk while discarding Skim milk. Lower cutoffs at deeper levels can reveal specific patterns, but they change which comparisons are fair.
stages.receiptHtml:
The lecture’s hierarchy, expressed per 100 transactions

Milk10%PassPass
2% milk6%PassPass

The “2%” in 2% milk names its fat category. Its observed support here is 6%.

For this simplified drawing the two subtypes are disjoint and fill the Milk total. In real baskets, subtype supports can overlap and must not automatically be added.

Source basis: Lecture pp.46–48; seminar slides 48–50. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Lower the child cutoff from 5% to 3%. Watch Skim milk cross the boundary. Keep the parent cutoff at 5% and distinguish those two settings.
stages.whyHtml:
Multilevel association mining uses a taxonomy such as Dairy → Milk → Skim milk. More specific items often need lower support thresholds.

Rules involving ancestor and descendant categories can be redundant. The lecture compares Milk → Wheat bread (70% confidence) with 2% milk → Wheat bread (72%). A small improvement may contribute little new information once the broad rule and relative subtype prevalence are considered.

Quantitative association mining makes numeric conditions into items: for example Age=34–35 and Income=30–50K → TV purchase. The next section works through discretization using the practical’s purchase-value idea.
stages.check: Should a rule Milk → Skim milk be interpreted as an independent shopping discovery?
stages.solution: Be careful. Skim milk is already a subtype of Milk, so the relationship partly reflects the taxonomy. It can be structurally trivial rather than useful new shopping evidence.
stages.referent: Percentage-point cells contain the six-blue/four-purple subtype decomposition; labelled parent and child support cutoffs differ.
stages.action: Move only the subtype minimum-support line
stages.nextReason: Categories can be items; numeric bands can too. Next make both into clear yes/no columns.

stages.title: Preprocessing creates the items
stages.question: What should one-hot encoding mean in the practical?
stages.answerHtml: A mining algorithm needs clear yes/no items. One-hot encoding makes one Boolean column per item: True means present, False means absent. Define the row’s unit, remove IDs, and turn numeric ranges into named items when needed. The practical’s BlackFriday rows are product records, so their rules concern those records’ categories and purchase bands.
stages.receiptHtml:
Two different input formats

InputPreparation
Sample Data.csvDrop transID. Replace documented ? absence with 0. Validate only 0/1, then cast to bool.
BlackFriday.csvKeep product categories and Purchase. Use qcut for three purchase bands. Build one token per category and band.
Invented row P7: Purchase=2,100; categories 1 and 8
Tokens: Cat=1, Cat=8, Purchase=High
Those three columns become True; the other columns become False.

The lab uses 9 invented product rows to show the mechanics. They are not the missing BlackFriday data. Its purchase thirds have boundaries 1,100 and 1,900.

Source basis: Practical pp.1–2,6–10. Reading receipts stay fixed when you edit the live lab.
stages.experiment: Select P7: predict which category and purchase-band columns become True. Then select P1, which has no extra category, and toggle “Encode no extra category”. Watch NoExtraCategory change from an omitted column to a present token. Compare P1’s Low band with P7’s High band.
stages.whyHtml:
In the small sample, the practical explicitly defines ? as absence. An unknown or unobserved value in another dataset must not automatically become False.

pd.qcut creates quantile bands with roughly equal counts, using the empirical data distribution. pd.cut uses chosen numeric boundaries. Tied values can make quantile boundaries non-unique and need an explicit handling policy.

Use tokens such as Cat=1 and Purchase=High so numeric categories cannot collide with numeric bin labels. Collapsing category-slot labels into Cat=1 means “category 1 appears in any slot”. If slot position matters, retain prefixes such as Category_1=1 instead.

The practical’s zero sentinel denotes no extra category, not product category zero. Keeping an explicit absence token is a deliberate modelling choice. It can dominate output with predictable rules. One-hot encoding also makes mutually exclusive purchase bands unable to co-occur in one record.

Neither Sample Data.csv nor BlackFriday.csv was supplied in this week’s folder. The companion script includes the four documented sample rows and accepts the real BlackFriday file later, without fabricating its results.

The companion’s NoExtraCategory token means both extra category slots are absent. This is a more specific meaning than the practical’s generic zero sentinel, which can appear when either extra slot is absent.

For these nine sorted prices, qcut places three records in each band. Its cut values interpolate empirical quantiles: 1,100 lies between 900 and 1,200; 1,900 lies between 1,800 and 2,100. The bands describe similar row counts, not equal numeric widths.
stages.check: Can these product-record rules establish which two distinct products share one customer basket?
stages.solution: No. A row contains one product record and its attributes. Basket-level product recommendations require a justified transaction or grouping unit with multiple products per basket.
stages.referent: Record dots occupy quantile bands; raw category and purchase values become named tokens and Boolean presence bits.
stages.action: Inspect a toy row and choose whether absence becomes an explicit item
stages.nextReason: The input now has a clear meaning. Next feed that Boolean representation into runnable Python.

stages.title: A small Python workflow
stages.question: How do the calculations become runnable code?
stages.answerHtml: Return to the four original shopping baskets. The Boolean table is the input; frequent itemsets are the first output; rules are the second. Apriori and FP-growth should agree on the same data and support threshold. They search differently, then apply the same confidence calculation.
stages.receiptHtml:
Complete four-basket Python example

Install the optional libraries in your Python environment with python3 -m pip install pandas mlxtend. Copy this complete example, or use the companion below.

import pandas as pd
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import (
    apriori, association_rules)

# 1. Presence rows, without transaction IDs
encoded = pd.DataFrame([
    [1, 0, 1, 1, 0],  # basket 100
    [0, 1, 1, 0, 1],  # basket 200
    [1, 1, 1, 0, 1],  # basket 300
    [0, 1, 0, 0, 1],  # basket 400
], columns=["Apple", "Bread", "Coke",
            "DVD", "Egg"], dtype=bool)

# 2. Itemsets with at least 50% support
freq = apriori(encoded,
    min_support=0.5, use_colnames=True)

# 3. Rules with at least 90% confidence
rules = association_rules(freq,
    metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.9,
    num_itemsets=len(encoded))
rules = rules.sort_values("lift", ascending=False)
print(len(freq), len(rules))  # 9 5

encoded is the yes/no input table; freq holds itemsets and supports; rules holds arrows and their scores. The example prints 9 5. The lab follows your current basket edits, while this printed example uses the fixed source rows.

Download the runnable Python companion. It also checks the practical’s MP3 rows and accepts real CSV files later.

API reference: mlxtend Apriori, association_rules, and FP-growth. Checked 1 October 2026.
stages.experiment: Follow the Boolean input through the itemset count bars into the rule table. Switch Apriori to FP-growth while keeping the thresholds fixed. Predict whether the output changes. If your current lab differs from the printed example, reset the baskets and thresholds to the source defaults.
stages.whyHtml:
To read the code: import loads tools; a name before = stores a result. The inner lists are rows, columns names the items, and dtype=bool turns 1/0 into True/False. A call such as apriori(...) runs a tool with the supplied input and settings. The comments mark the same three steps shown in the visual.

use_colnames=True preserves readable item names. max_len limits the length of mined itemsets, not the number of rules. The confidence cutoff belongs to association_rules, rather than to apriori.

The code includes num_itemsets, as shown in current mlxtend examples. The companion inspects the function signature so it also works with earlier installations that lack that argument.

For the small practical CSV, validate values before astype(bool): the string "0" is truthy in Python, so casting raw strings directly is unsafe.

The optional BlackFriday path selects the documented columns, validates Purchase, bins into Low/Medium/High, preserves absent extra categories explicitly if requested, encodes tokens with TransactionEncoder, and compares both miners. It reports itemsets and rule metrics calculated from the actual file.
stages.check: If Apriori and FP-growth return different supports on identical input, is that expected?
stages.solution: No. Their output values should agree for the same itemsets, data, and threshold. Investigate preprocessing, parameters, or implementation differences.
stages.referent: The four-by-five Boolean input feeds the selected exact miner’s frequent counts and corresponding rule table.
stages.action: Switch algorithms and alter the shared thresholds
stages.nextReason: The program returns rules. Next decide what their evidence can support and what still needs a separate test.

stages.title: Use evidence, then choose an action
stages.question: What would make a discovered rule useful?
stages.answerHtml: A useful rule connects a credible pattern with a concrete question. Check the transaction unit, co-occurrence count, baseline, novelty, and practical value. A rule can suggest a test of a bundle or recommendation. Measuring the effect of that action needs new evidence.

stages.experiment: Start with “Lift and an action”: compare the ketchup baseline with its frequency among burger records, then decide what the rule can establish. Try the other revision questions. Use the visible evidence before choosing an answer; the feedback explains your result.
stages.whyHtml:
Actionable rules point toward a useful decision. Trivial rules restate known facts, such as a category hierarchy. Inexplicable rules may deserve investigation but do not immediately imply a worthwhile action.

Rare patterns can have large lift with very few joint observations. Keep absolute counts visible. Evaluate whether patterns persist in fresh periods, whether many comparisons were searched, and whether the item definitions create the relationship mechanically.

The laboratory uses exact counts for small teaching datasets. It performs no sales forecasting, causal estimation, or significance test. A production system also needs scale, monitoring, and evaluation of decisions made from its rules.

Reading clarifications

Seminar slide 56’s repeated CPU in the lift numerator is a typo: the numerator is the CPU/GPU joint support. At slide 61, the 67% reverse rules fail the stated 90% cutoff. The four sample rows give nine frequent itemsets at 50% support, despite the practical’s prose saying eight. FP-growth is designed for scalable mining, with data-dependent speed and memory demands. χ² > 1 is not a general significance threshold.
stages.check: Would lift 3.33 prove a burger promotion causes ketchup sales to rise?
stages.solution: No. It describes conditional co-occurrence relative to a baseline in observed records. A causal promotion effect requires an appropriate experiment or justified causal study.
stages.referent: The initial revision scene compares ketchup’s 10% baseline with 50/150 conditional occurrence; each other problem has its own count evidence and legend.
